record.title: McMorris Interview with Pham Xuan An (Part 1)

point.title: Greetings and Light Conversations
point.partial_transcript: Alright. Ok. Are you on the—you said you're on the Fulbright scholarship?
point.synopsis: After a brief introduction with Phạm Xuân Hoàng Ân, Phạm Xuân Ẩn's eldest son, Sean McMorris and Hoàng Ân talked about their academic experiences and endeavors. McMorris explained that his purpose in Vietnam is to learn and record the Vietnamese perspective of the Vietnam War as well as give people a more realistic view of post-war Vietnam. McMorris and Phạm Xuân Ẩn also talked about recent events in Vietnam at the time, such as the Bill Clinton visit, the Dien Bien Phu anniversary and the return of many important figures.
point.keywords: Fulbright Scholarship; Pham Xuan An; Phạm Xuân Ẩn; Bill Clinton; Bobby Mueller; Battle of Dien Bien Phu; Dien Bien Phu; Pham Xuan Hoang An; Phạm Xuân Hoàng Ân

point.title: American Ideology, Foreign Intervention, and Vietnamese Resistance in early Vietnam War
point.partial_transcript: What was your role during the war? During the American war after the French had left, and America had come in
point.synopsis: An begins by recounting the early stages of American involvement in the Indochinese conflict. An explained how South Vietnam went from French-backed to American-backed. Pham Xuan An, through his work with the American military training mission, explains one of the motivations of US intervention in Vietnam: U.S. ideology of self-determination of colonized countries and Wilsonian idealism, which it has applied in other areas around the world after World War 2. However, these ideals contrasted with colonial realities and Stalinist Soviet politics. Vietnamese nationalists felt trapped in the paradox of American and Soviet support, each vying for control. While unable to react to the Soviet contradiction, they were able to lead protests towards American intervention, leading to a turning point in 1950 toward resisting both French and American intervention.
point.keywords: Wilsonianism; Wilsonian idealism; World War 2; WW2; Soviet Union; USSR; Joseph Stalin; Nikita Khrushchev; MAAG; Military Assistance Advisory Group; Edward Lansdale; Ngo Dinh Diem

point.title: The Vietnam War v.s. Previous 20th Century Conflicts
point.partial_transcript: What made the American—Vietnam War different than World War One, World War Two, as far as fighting it?
point.synopsis: The dialogue discusses why the Vietnam War differed from earlier U.S. wars. Pham Xuan An explains that anti-colonial wars in Vietnam were supported by China and the Soviet Union, creating a “war of liberation” that the U.S. had to confront, unlike previous colonial conflicts where America had limited involvement. While it appeared the U.S. repeated France’s mistakes, An argues circumstances were different: France was compelled to accept Vietnamese independence for financial and strategic reasons because of its unfortunate position during WWII, while post-WWII Americans faced a new global context. The U.S. could not allow European powers to regain influence in Asia, leading to a politically driven intervention that set a precedent for later conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan.
point.keywords: WWI; WWII; World War I; World War II; Iraq; Afghanistan; Russia; France; Germany; China; USSR; Soviet Union; Japan; War of Liberation

point.title: Post–Cold War U.S. Interventions, Oil Politics, and the Use of Pretexts
point.partial_transcript: Still dealing with the after-effects of the collapse of communist—the Soviet Union.
point.synopsis: Pham Xuan An argues that after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the United States continued frequent military interventions driven by long-term geopolitical and economic interests, particularly control over oil. He describes a pattern of repeated wars that are costly, destabilizing, and difficult to reconstruct, often justified through political pretexts rather than transparent causes. An links interventions in the Middle East, and Central Asia to fears of rival powers such as Russia and China gaining influence as well as the inability to shift from Cold War mindsets. He compares Iraq to Vietnam, emphasizing that while tactics may differ, U.S. strategy remains shaped by politics, resource security, and the strategic construction of justifications for war. McMorris then asks why the Vietnam war was such an important turning point in American history, and to that, An responded that the war on terror is different than the earlier Cold War against the USSR because it is not a war against communism but a war against theory, ideology, and politics of the Arab World.
point.keywords: OPEC; Iraq; Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries; Middle East; Kuwait; Central Asia; Cold War; China; Ted Kennedy; Gulf of Tonkin Incident; USS Maddox; Pre-text; Pretext; War on Terror; Terrorism

point.title: Vietnam and the US in the Cold War Context
point.partial_transcript: What fascinates me is how Americans cannot forget the Vietnam War. It was such an important time period in American history that one person told me, not only did it—they said, it changed America as much as it changed Vietnam, and the war was fought on Vietnamese soil.
point.synopsis: McMorris suggests that South Vietnam may have “won” the war since present-day Vietnam is moving toward a free-market economy and loosening state control. Pham Xuan An disagrees, arguing that Vietnam’s true objective was national independence, not ideological victory. That independence, however, came with hard lessons: reliance on the Soviet Union and China weakened Vietnam’s position at the Geneva Conference. By the Paris Peace Talks, North Vietnam therefore sought to negotiate directly with the United States and minimize external influence. An situates these talks within America’s Wilsonian doctrine of self-determination, which guided U.S. global strategy after both world wars and shaped institutions such as the UN, IMF, World Bank, and GATT. This vision collapsed due to the Cold War after 1947, leading the U.S. to contain communism through Southeast Asian alliances, intelligence operations, and regional proxies/interventions. Meanwhile, instability in South Vietnam undermined U.S. efforts, but America successfully set up ASEAN with South Vietnam under the Thieu regime. Facing pressure from both war and communist allies, North Vietnam launched the Tet Offensive to force negotiations, successfully pushing the U.S. toward talks.
point.keywords: Russia; China; USSR; Soviet Union; Cold War; Wilsonianism; North Vietnam; South Vietnam; Southeast Asia; United States of America; negotiations; political pressure; independence; Nguyễn Văn Thiệu; Nguyen Van Thieu

point.title: Scholarship on the Vietnam War
point.partial_transcript: So there was a time period between—was it in the 1980s when they allowed the freedom of press to come out and all of the books like I know Duong Thu Huong [Dương Thu Hương] and Bao Ninh [Hoàng Ấu Phương, pen name Bảo Ninh] and stuff.
point.synopsis: McMorris asks about the freedom of press in Vietnam during the 1980s, to which An emphasizes that understanding Vietnam requires broad and sustained study. He notes that many books, both Vietnamese and international, now examine the war from multiple perspectives. An highlights the importance of scholarly research institutions in the United States, particularly a Vietnam-focused center at Texas Tech University. He explains that this institution, led by James R. Reckner with Douglas Pike as co-director, became a major repository for Vietnam War research after Pike transferred his extensive archives from UC Berkeley due to funding limitations. The center houses tens of thousands of books and documents from diverse international sources, including the Soviet Union, China, France, and Britain. An strongly recommends it as a valuable resource for serious research. McMorris adds that the center continues to expand its collection by gathering personal materials such as letters from war veterans, preserving a comprehensive historical record of the war.
point.keywords: scholarship; Texas Tech University; TTU; James R. Recker; Douglas E. Pike; research; Vietnam War scholarship

point.title: Vietnam's Adjustment to State-Controlled Market Economy
point.partial_transcript: So back to your story. So that's why you want to understand this side. You talked to those who really know because there are many of them, they think they know, but they don't know.
point.synopsis: An expresses his concern over the people who lack a visionary view. He goes on to explain that there are two types of policies in the US: pragmatic and visionary policies. After the war, Vietnam struggled to transition to a market economy. Former capitalist elites can't be used in the new market economy era because they lacked knowledge of modern capitalism and were persecuted, while younger generations were unprepared for globalization. Many former soldiers were disappointed when socialist ideals were not realized. An maintains that postwar policies like re-education camps were unavoidable within a communist system. He expresses no personal regrets, viewing the war as a necessary historical struggle for Vietnamese independence, charaterized by difficult but inevitable adjustments to new realities.
point.keywords: Visionary policy; Pragmatic policy; Capitalism; Market economy; Generational differences; Adapting

point.title: Reflections on War and Peace in Vietnam and Asia
point.partial_transcript: What would you would you like—like my generation and people in America—to know about Vietnam today? Because a lot of us don't know anything about Vietnam today.
point.synopsis: When asked about what Americans should know about Vietnam today, An stated that we must learn to move beyond hatred. At the end of the day, everyone was a victim of American policy/policymakers and all suffered. He hopes that the countries and its people can renew their friendship and let the younger generations live happily, if they are lucky, If they aren't lucky, wars will continue to go on. He then pivots to lament about 9/11 and the start of the war in Afghanistan. An express sorrow about how his hope for peace was broken and how he feels horrible about the innocent people that died. He recollects how his life was filled with wars, from Japanese imperialism in Vietnam to World War 2 to the Cold War. However, An also acknowledges the political complexity in the Arabian conflicts, how the conflict is a result of western imperialism and internal corruption, tying it back to American involvement in the Vietnam War.
point.keywords: 9/11; September 11; imperialism; reconciliation; war; Arab world; Afghanistan; peace; hopes
